problem: Prior GCRL + CBS multi-agent visual navigation prunes edges whose predicted risk exceeds a local threshold before planning. This binary pruning is overly conservative and makes missions infeasible when goals need hazardous regions, even if aggregate risk is acceptable.
motivation: Safety-critical multi-agent navigation from visual observations needs budgeted risk acceptance rather than strict avoidance. A single global risk budget lets some agents take more risk while others stay safe, and gives users one knob for the safety-efficiency trade-off.
key_idea: Keep all edges of the learned waypoint graph and add an Iterative Risk Allocation layer to CBS that redistributes per-agent risk budgets under a shared global bound, using either a greedy surplus-deficit scheme (EQUIRIS) or a Walrasian price-based market (WALRIS).
insight: The ability to reallocate risk during search is what matters: a Constant allocation with no reallocation gets zero success, while Uniform, Utility and Inverse-Utility initializations perform near identically. WALRIS's price bisection explores the allocation space more thoroughly than EQUIRIS's single transfer, giving shorter paths at medium-to-high budgets and better success at the tightest budget and with 10 agents.
method: Problem formulation (Δ-MAPF): minimize sum of path lengths over a learned distance/risk waypoint graph subject to a total risk sum ≤ Δ; no risk-based edge pruning.
Learned graph: dual distance and risk critics from GCRL (following Feng et al. 2025) score edges between replay-buffer states.
High-level CBS with risk state: each constraint-tree node stores per-agent budgets δ and validity flags φ; a failed low-level replan triggers ReallocateRisk.

Low-level risk-bounded A*: search over (node, accumulated risk) states with dominance pruning to find the shortest path with ρ ≤ δ_i; auxiliary MinFeasibleRisk and LenMinRisk A* queries give per-agent lower and upper budget bounds.
Initial allocation: Uniform (Δ/N), Utility-based, or Inverse-utility-based at the root.

EQUIRIS: computes total deficit of failing agents and surplus of passing agents, prunes the node if the deficit exceeds the surplus, otherwise gives failing agents their minimum risk and deducts greedily from donors.

WALRIS: bisects a scalar price of risk p; each agent picks δ from a small neighborhood minimizing length + p·risk via risk-bounded A*; p is raised or lowered depending on whether total risk exceeds Δ, and the best feasible allocation is kept.

setting.backbone: Goal-conditioned RL actor with distance and risk distributional critics (conv + FC), trained from scratch; planning is CBS + risk-bounded A* with the IRA layer
setting.training_data: GCRL trained in-scene from the agent's own replay buffer (100k buffer, 600k iterations) with self-supervised curriculum goal sampling; no external data
setting.observation: 32x32 RGB from four cardinal directions concatenated into a panorama (visual tasks); (x,y) state in 2D
setting.action_space: continuous 2D displacement (dx,dy) in [-1,1]^2 executed by the GCRL policy toward planner waypoints on a graph
setting.simulator: Habitat-Sim with ReplicaCAD scenes; 2D point environment; ROS2/Gazebo and Crazyflie hardware demos
setting.privileged: none at test time; the risk-bound calibration [Δ_low, Δ_high] uses auxiliary CBS runs for benchmarking only

numbers_note: Results appear only in figures (success rate, average steps, cumulative risk vs Δ) and in text; no results tables. Only the text-stated EQUIRIS success rates at the tightest budget (74% in 2D, 76% visual) are given, and this is a custom benchmark not in the canonical list.
results: Both strategies beat Constrained Risk, Lagrangian and Bi-Objective (MO-CBS) baselines in success rate across risk levels. Success degrades only at the tightest budget, where EQUIRIS drops to 74% (2D) and 76% (visual) and WALRIS is more robust. Average steps decrease monotonically as Δ increases, WALRIS finds shorter paths than EQUIRIS, and the trends persist from 5 to 10 agents.
limitations: No completeness or optimality guarantees: both allocation heuristics can prune feasible nodes or converge to local optima.
Relies on the fidelity of learned critics, so Δ bounds only predicted risk, and the fixed replay-buffer graphs limit generalization to unseen scenes.
CBS-based, so exponential worst case in the number of agents (tested only up to 10).
builds_on: Safe multi-agent navigation guided by GCRL + CBS (Feng et al. 2025)
